sections.h2: What is a transfer on death deed in Washington?
sections.html:
It is a recorded deed that names who receives your real estate when you die while leaving you full control of the property until then. Chapter 64.80 RCW, the Washington uniform real property transfer on death act, authorizes it: under RCW 64.80.020 an individual may transfer property to one or more beneficiaries effective at the transferor's death by a transfer on death deed.

The statute calls the deed nontestamentary (RCW 64.80.040), so it is not a will, yet it carries the same capacity standard. The person who makes or revokes one needs the capacity required to make a will (RCW 64.80.050). The act applies to deeds made before, on or after June 12, 2014, for owners who die on or after that date (RCW 64.80.901), and it does not displace other lawful ways of passing property (RCW 64.80.902).

sections.h2: What must a Washington transfer on death deed contain?
sections.html:
It must look like an ordinary recordable deed, say that the transfer happens at your death, and be recorded before you die. RCW 64.80.060 sets three requirements:

  • It contains the essential elements and formalities of a properly recordable deed made during life.
  • It states that the transfer to the designated beneficiary is to occur at the transferor's death.
  • It is recorded before the transferor's death with the auditor of the county where the property is located.

A deed signed but never recorded does not meet the third requirement. Recording also brings in the first-page rules for any recorded instrument: a three-inch top margin, a return address, the document title, grantor and grantee names, an abbreviated legal description and the assessor's parcel number (RCW 65.04.045). The beneficiary does not need to be told, does not need to accept, and does not need to give anything in return (RCW 64.80.070).

The act also bars one use. A transfer on death deed may not serve as a deed in lieu of foreclosure of a deed of trust (RCW 64.80.020).

sections.h2: What can the owner still do while alive?
sections.html:
Almost everything. During your life the deed does not affect your rights or those of any other owner, including the right to sell or borrow against the property (RCW 64.80.090). It also does not create any legal or equitable interest for the beneficiary, and it does not expose the property to the beneficiary's creditors. Your creditors, present and future, keep the same rights they had, even if they know about the deed.

The deed does not affect your eligibility, or the beneficiary's, for any form of public assistance while you are alive. Selling the house while you are alive simply ends the deed's effect, since the transfer applies only to property you own at death (RCW 64.80.100).

The deed is revocable even if it says otherwise (RCW 64.80.030). To revoke, RCW 64.80.080 requires a new instrument that does one of these things:

  • A later transfer on death deed that revokes the earlier one expressly or by inconsistency.
  • A separate instrument of revocation that expressly revokes it.
  • An inter vivos deed that expressly revokes it.

Whichever form you use, you must acknowledge it after the acknowledgment of the deed being revoked, and record it before your death in the county where the first deed is recorded. Marking up or tearing the recorded deed does nothing. If several owners signed, revocation by one does not touch the others' interests, and a deed of community property by both spouses or domestic partners is revoked only by both, unless only one is still living.

sections.h2: What happens to the house at the owner's death?
sections.html:
Title moves to the beneficiary named in the deed, but only if that person outlives you. Under RCW 64.80.100 the interest of a beneficiary who fails to survive lapses. With several beneficiaries, shares pass in equal and undivided parts with no right of survivorship, and a lapsed share goes to the others in proportion to what each holds.

Situation at deathWhat RCW 64.80.100 provides
Beneficiary outlives ownerInterest passes under the deed
Beneficiary dies firstThat beneficiary's interest lapses
Owner was a joint owner with survivorsProperty goes to the surviving joint owners by survivorship
Owner was the last surviving joint ownerThe deed takes effect
Community property, spouse did not join the deedOwner's interest passes under the deed
Community property, spouse joined and survivesThe deed is not effective at that death

Source: RCW 64.80.100 (app.leg.wa.gov).

The beneficiary takes the property subject to every mortgage, lien and contract already on it at the owner's death. That includes liens recorded within twenty-four months after death under RCW 41.05A.090 and 43.20B.080. The transfer comes without covenant or warranty of title, even if the deed says otherwise. A beneficiary is also liable for allowed claims against the probate estate and statutory allowances to a surviving spouse and children, to the extent chapter 64.80 and the cross-referenced estate statutes provide (RCW 64.80.120), and may disclaim all or part of the interest under chapter 11.86 RCW.

sections.h2: Is real estate excise tax due when a transfer on death deed takes effect?
sections.html:
Generally no. The Department of Revenue rule on inheritance, WAC 458-61A-202, exempts a transfer made under a previously recorded transfer on death deed when the owner dies. The paperwork is a certified copy of the death certificate, provided to the county treasurer where the property sits and recorded with the county auditor. There is one exception: if the transfer satisfies a contractual obligation the owner owed to the beneficiary, the tax is due.

The exemption stops at the beneficiary. A later sale by an heir to someone else is a taxable sale, according to the same rule. The Department's real estate excise tax page says the seller usually pays, the tax is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale, and exemptions are claimed by listing a code on the affidavit.

sections.h2: How does a transfer on death deed compare with other routes for a Washington house?
sections.html:
Because a transfer on death deed is nontestamentary, it is one of several tools, and the act itself says it does not limit other methods of passing property (RCW 64.80.902). A will that goes through probate involves a court-appointed personal representative, and the rule on nonpro rata distributions notes that a representative with nonintervention powers may distribute under RCW 11.68.090 without excise tax when no consideration is paid.

The small estate affidavit under RCW 11.62.010 is a different tool. It lets a successor collect debts and personal property that are subject to probate, when the probate estate does not exceed $100,000 less liens and encumbrances, excluding a surviving spouse's community interest, and forty days have passed since the death. That statute speaks of debts and personal property, so check with a Washington attorney before assuming it moves a house.

If you have inherited a house under a transfer on death deed and want to sell without repairs, listing or cleanout, a cash buyer can work from the recorded deed and death certificate. Ask the county auditor and a title company what needs to be recorded first.

faqs.q: Do I have to record a Washington transfer on death deed before I die?
faqs.a: Yes. RCW 64.80.060 requires recording with the auditor of the county where the property is located before the transferor's death. A deed signed but not recorded in time does not meet the statute.

faqs.q: Can I change my mind after recording a transfer on death deed?
faqs.a: Yes. The deed is revocable even if it says it is not. You revoke it with a later transfer on death deed, an instrument of revocation or a deed that expressly revokes it, acknowledged and recorded in the same county before you die.

faqs.q: Does the beneficiary have to be told about the deed?
faqs.a: No. The deed is effective without notice to, delivery to or acceptance by the designated beneficiary during your life, and without any payment or other consideration (RCW 64.80.070).

faqs.q: What if my beneficiary dies before I do?
faqs.a: That beneficiary's interest lapses. If you named several beneficiaries, the lapsed share goes to the others in proportion to their interests in the remaining property (RCW 64.80.100).

faqs.q: Does the beneficiary owe excise tax when the house passes at death?
faqs.a: Generally not. WAC 458-61A-202 exempts a transfer under a recorded transfer on death deed and asks for a certified death certificate. Tax is due if the transfer satisfies a contractual obligation the owner had to the beneficiary.
